text: Social media management goes beyond simply posting content. Most business leaders think of it as scheduling posts for Facebook or Instagram, but true management involves strategy, analytics, engagement, and much more. As social channels continue to evolve, the role of social media management grows increasingly complex and vital for business success. I’ve seen this evolution firsthand in my work with organizations of all sizes. Social media has transformed from a nice-to-have marketing channel into a mission-critical business function that directly impacts brand perception, customer relationships, and bottom-line results. In this article, we’ll explore what social media management truly encompasses, why it matters for your business, and how to approach it strategically. Whether you’re just starting out or looking to refine your existing approach, you’ll gain actionable insights into effective social media management. Key Takeaways ✅ Social media management covers far more than posting content. It’s the coordinated practice of strategy, content creation, community engagement, analytics, and paid social, all pointed at the same business goals. ✅ The discipline breaks into five core components: strategy development, content creation, community management, analytics and reporting, and paid social advertising. Each one feeds the next in a continuous cycle. ✅ The social media manager role is multidisciplinary. One person or a specialized team owns strategy, publishing, engagement, reporting, trend monitoring, and crisis response. That scope expands as the organization grows. ✅ Done well, social media management delivers measurable business outcomes: website traffic, qualified leads, stronger customer loyalty, and first-party audience insights. The payoff reaches well past brand visibility. ✅ The next phase of the discipline is being shaped by AI-assisted workflows, social commerce, and short-form video, plus tighter privacy rules. Those rules reward owned communities and first-party data over raw reach. Defining Social Media Management Social media management refers to the process of creating, scheduling, analyzing, and engaging with content posted on social media platforms. It encompasses everything from developing comprehensive strategies to day-to-day community management. At its core, social media management aims to strengthen brand presence, build community, drive engagement, and ultimately achieve specific business objectives through social channels. This process requires both creative and analytical skills, combining content creation with data-driven decision-making. The scope of social media management has expanded dramatically in recent years. What once focused primarily on organic content now includes paid advertising, i nfluencer collaborations , social listening , crisis management, and customer service functions. Today’s consumers increasingly turn to social media before making purchase decisions. In fact, 63% of Gen Zs get product recommendations from social media platforms. This shift in consumer behavior has elevated social media from a mere marketing channel to a central touchpoint in the customer journey, making effective management more crucial than ever for business success. The Core Components of Social Media Management Social media management comprises several key components that work together to create a cohesive approach. Understanding these components helps clarify what comprehensive management entails beyond just posting content. The following table outlines the five core components of social media management, their primary functions, and why each matters to your overall social media success: Component Primary Functions Business Impact Strategy Development Goal-setting, audience research, platform selection, content planning Provides direction and measurable objectives for all activities Content Creation Writing, design, video production, curation, scheduling Builds brand voice and drives audience engagement Community Management Responding to comments, messages, mentions; moderation Strengthens relationships and customer loyalty Analytics & Reporting Tracking metrics, performance analysis, insights generation Informs strategy refinement and demonstrates ROI Paid Social Media Ad creation, audience targeting, budget management, A/B testing Extends reach and accelerates results Let’s explore each of these components in greater depth: Strategy Development Strategy forms the foundation of effective social media management. This process starts with defining clear, measurable goals that align with broader business objectives. Are you focused on brand awareness, community building, lead generation, or customer service? A well-developed strategy includes detailed audience research to understand who you’re trying to reach, which platforms they use, and what content resonates with them. This research informs platform selection, ensuring you focus resources where your audience actually spends time. The strategy component also includes developing content themes, voice guidelines, and editorial calendars that maintain consistency while adapting to each platform’s unique environment. Content Creation and Curation Content remains the fuel that powers social media engagement. This component encompasses creating original content, adapting it for different platforms, and curating relevant third-party content that adds value for your audience. Effective content creation requires understanding platform-specific best practices. For example, the visual storytelling that works on Instagram differs significantly from the professional insights that perform well on LinkedIn. Content planning also includes determining optimal posting frequencies and times. Global social media users spend an average of 2 hours and 24 minutes daily on social platforms, making timing an important consideration for visibility. Community Engagement and Monitoring Social media is fundamentally social. The engagement component focuses on building relationships through active participation in conversations with your audience. This includes responding to comments, answering questions, and acknowledging mentions. Speed matters in this component. Most consumers today expect quick responses, with 68% expecting brands to respond to social media messages within 24 hours. Community management also involves monitoring for brand mentions across platforms, even when you’re not directly tagged. This practice helps identify customer service issues, potential crises, and opportunities to join relevant conversations. Make LinkedIn Your Best Source of Clients My latest book helps professionals, entrepreneurs, and business owners turn LinkedIn from a static profile into a real source of clients and growth. Maximizing LinkedIn for Business Growth gives you clear, practical steps to build a profile that gets noticed and a network that actually sends business your way. Grab your copy on Amazon and put it to work this week. Click the cover or the button below to get started. Analytics and Reporting Data drives effective social media management. The analytics component includes tracking key performance indicators, analyzing content performance, and generating actionable insights to refine your approach. Regular reporting helps demonstrate the value of social media efforts to stakeholders while providing the feedback needed to optimize future content and campaigns. This process connects social media activities to tangible business outcomes. Analytics also enables testing different approaches to determine what works best for your specific audience and goals. This data-driven approach maximizes return on both time and financial investments in social media. Paid Social Media Advertising As organic reach has declined across platforms, paid social has become an essential component of comprehensive social media management. Global social media ad spending is projected to reach $276.7 billion , highlighting its growing importance. This component includes creating compelling ad content, defining target audiences, managing budgets, and optimizing campaigns based on performance data. Effective paid social integrates seamlessly with organic efforts, amplifying overall impact. Advanced social media management approaches use paid advertising strategically to support specific goals while maintaining a healthy balance with organic content and engagement. The Role of a Social Media Manager A social media manager orchestrates all aspects of a brand’s social media presence. This multifaceted role requires diverse skills spanning creative content development, analytical thinking, and strategic planning. Here are the core responsibilities that professional social media managers handle: Strategy development and implementation – Creating roadmaps for social media success aligned with business goals Content creation and curation – Producing engaging posts adapted to each platform’s unique environment Community management – Building relationships through timely responses and proactive engagement Performance analysis – Tracking metrics, generating reports, and extracting actionable insights Trend monitoring – Staying current with platform changes and emerging content formats Crisis management – Addressing negative situations quickly and appropriately Paid social campaign management – Creating and optimizing advertising to extend reach Effective social media managers balance these varied responsibilities while adapting to the constantly evolving social landscape. They must understand both the technical aspects of each platform and the nuanced ways different audiences engage with content. The scope of social media management varies based on organization size. In smaller companies, one person might handle all social media functions, while larger enterprises often have specialized teams focusing on specific platforms or components like content creation or analytics. Let’s examine how different platforms require specialized management approaches: Platform Primary Audience Content Focus Management Priorities Facebook Diverse demographic, 25-54 primary Text, images, videos, links, events Community building, groups, paid targeting Instagram Visual-focused, 18-34 primarily High-quality images, Stories, Reels Visual storytelling, hashtag strategy LinkedIn Professionals, B2B focus Industry insights, company news Thought leadership, networking, employee advocacy TikTok Gen Z, younger millennials Short-form video, trending content Creative authenticity, trend participation YouTube Broad reach across demographics Long-form and short-form video Content quality, SEO, community engagement This table highlights why effective social media management requires platform-specific expertise. YouTube, for instance, leads global social media platform usage according to demographic research. Each platform has unique algorithms , audience expectations, and content formats that successful social media managers must navigate skillfully to maximize results. Benefits of Effective Social Media Management Properly managed social media delivers numerous advantages beyond simple brand visibility. Organizations that invest in comprehensive social media management typically see benefits across multiple business areas. Understanding these benefits helps frame social media management as a strategic business function rather than just a marketing activity. Here’s how effective management delivers value: Building Brand Awareness and Recognition Consistent, strategic social media presence significantly increases brand visibility. With 5.24 billion social media users projected globally, these platforms offer unparalleled reach potential. Effective management ensures your brand maintains a cohesive identity across platforms while adapting content to each environment’s unique characteristics. This consistency helps build recognition over time as audiences repeatedly encounter your brand voice, visual elements, and messaging. Beyond general awareness, strategic social media management positions your brand within specific conversations relevant to your industry, helping you reach precisely the audience segments most valuable to your business. Increasing Website Traffic and Leads Social media serves as a significant traffic driver when managed strategically. By sharing valuable content with clear calls to action, you create pathways from social platforms to your website where deeper engagement and conversion can occur. This traffic tends to be more engaged than some other sources because users have already connected with your content on social platforms before clicking through. The relationship foundation has already begun. For lead generation specifically, sophisticated social media management incorporates targeted campaigns designed to capture prospect information through content offers, contests, or direct response ads. Enhancing Customer Engagement and Loyalty Perhaps the most unique benefit of social media compared to other marketing channels is its ability to foster two-way communication. Effective management transforms these platforms from broadcast channels into community spaces. Regular engagement with followers builds relationships that extend beyond transactional interactions. Responding to comments, acknowledging user-generated content, and actively participating in conversations humanizes your brand. This engagement directly impacts loyalty. Customers who receive responses from brands on social media demonstrate higher satisfaction and stronger brand affinity than those who don’t experience such interactions. Providing Valuable Customer Insights Well-managed social media functions as an ongoing focus group, revealing customer preferences, pain points, and trends. Strategic social listening captures conversations about your brand, competitors, and industry. These insights extend beyond marketing to inform product development, customer service improvements, and even business strategy. They provide real-time feedback that traditional research methods might miss. Particularly valuable is the competitive intelligence aspect. Social media management tools enable benchmarking against competitors’ performance while identifying gaps and opportunities in the market. Social Media Management Tools and Platforms The complexity of managing multiple social accounts across various platforms has driven the development of specialized tools that streamline workflows and enhance results. These tools have become essential for efficient social media management. Different tools address specific aspects of the management process. The following table breaks down key categories and popular options in each: Tool Category Primary Functions Popular Tools Best For All-in-One Platforms Content scheduling, analytics, engagement management Hootsuite, Sprout Social, Buffer Teams needing comprehensive management in one dashboard Scheduling Tools Content calendar, multi-platform posting Later, SocialPilot, MeetEdgar Focus on content publishing efficiency Analytics Platforms Performance metrics, competitive analysis Google Analytics, Brandwatch, Keyhole Data-driven strategy refinement Social Listening Brand monitoring, conversation tracking Mention, Talkwalker, Brandwatch Reputation management and customer insights Content Creation Graphics, video, writing assistance Canva , Adobe Express, Lumen5 Streamlining visual content production When selecting tools for your social media management stack, consider these factors: The right tool combination depends on your specific needs, team size, content volume, and budget. Many organizations use multiple specialized tools rather than relying solely on all-in-one platforms. For teams with limited resources, prioritize tools that address your biggest pain points first. If content creation is your bottleneck, start with design tools. If analysis is your weakness, focus on analytics platforms. The tool landscape continues to evolve rapidly. Currently, 71% of marketers use AI-powered tools in their social media workflows to improve efficiency and results. Beyond third-party tools, each social platform offers native management features worth exploring. These platform-specific tools often provide unique capabilities not available through third-party solutions, particularly for advertising functions. A robust set of social media management tools often becomes the command center for your entire social media operation, making tool selection a strategic decision rather than merely a tactical one. Developing an Effective Social Media Strategy Strategic planning forms the foundation of successful social media management. Without a clear strategy, even the most engaging content or cutting-edge tools won’t deliver optimal results. A comprehensive social media strategy connects your social efforts to specific business goals while providing a roadmap for daily tactical decisions. Here’s how to develop this essential framework: Setting Clear Objectives Begin with defining specific, measurable goals for your social media presence. These objectives should align with broader business goals while being attainable through social channels. Common social media objectives include increasing brand awareness, driving website traffic, generating leads, supporting customer service, or building community. The key is selecting primary objectives rather than trying to accomplish everything simultaneously. For each objective, establish concrete key performance indicators (KPIs) that will measure success. These might include follower growth rate, engagement percentage, click-through rates, or social media-attributed conversions. Understanding Your Audience Audience research directly informs every aspect of your strategy. Define detailed personas for your target audience segments, including: Demographic information (age, location, occupation) Platform preferences and usage patterns Content consumption habits and preferences Pain points your business addresses Motivations for engaging with brands like yours This research should combine both quantitative data from analytics tools and qualitative insights from customer interactions. The depth of this understanding directly impacts content relevance and engagement. Pay special attention to generational differences in social media usage. For instance, GenZ is the only generation where a majority spend more than two hours a day on social media, potentially making them more reachable through these channels. Content Strategy Development Your content strategy outlines what you’ll publish, where, when, and why. This plan should address: Content themes and topics that align with audience interests and business expertise. The most effective strategies balance educational, entertaining, and promotional content rather than focusing solely on self-promotion. Platform-specific content approaches. Each social network has unique content formats and audience expectations. For example, TikTok’s 2.50% engagement rate exceeds most other platforms , but requires specific content styles. A well-structured content calendar that maintains consistency while allowing flexibility for timely topics. This calendar should outline posting frequency, content categories, and responsibility assignments. Implementation Planning The implementation phase translates strategy into action by establishing: Clear workflows for content creation, approval, publishing, and engagement management. These processes should define roles, responsibilities, and timelines. Resource allocation decisions covering budget, personnel, and tools. Effective resource planning ensures your ambitions match your available resources. Training and skill development plans to address any capability gaps on your team. As social media constantly evolves, ongoing learning is essential. A well-crafted social media strategy serves as a decision-making framework that keeps daily activities aligned with long-term business goals. It provides both direction and accountability for your social media management efforts. Measuring Social Media Management Success Effective measurement transforms social media from a perceived “soft” marketing activity into a data-driven business function with demonstrable value. Strategic metrics connect social media efforts to business outcomes. Different objectives require different measurement approaches. This framework helps organize metrics based on common social media goals: Objective Key Metrics Measurement Tools Reporting Frequency Brand Awareness Reach, impressions, follower growth, share of voice Platform analytics, social listening tools Monthly Engagement Engagement rate, comments, shares, saves Platform analytics, social management tools Weekly Traffic Generation Click-through rate, website visits, bounce rate Google Analytics, UTM tracking Weekly Lead Generation Conversion rate, cost per lead, form completions CRM integration, landing page analytics Weekly/Monthly Sales/Revenue Attributed revenue, social commerce sales, ROI E-commerce analytics, multi-touch attribution Monthly/Quarterly Beyond these specific metrics, consider these measurement best practices: Focus on trends over time rather than isolated metrics. Month-over-month and year-over-year comparisons reveal progress patterns that single data points might obscure. Combine quantitative and qualitative measures for a complete picture. Numbers tell what happened, while sentiment analysis and conversation monitoring explain why. Connect social metrics to broader business KPIs whenever possible. This connection demonstrates social media’s contribution to organizational goals like customer acquisition or retention. The social commerce opportunity provides a tangible example of measurable business impact. U.S. social commerce sales are projected to surpass $100 billion in 2026 , creating direct revenue attribution opportunities for social media managers. Establish benchmarks for context . These might include your own historical performance, industry averages, or competitor metrics. Benchmarks provide crucial context for interpreting raw numbers. Effective measurement also requires proper tracking setup. Ensure you’ve implemented: UTM parameters for all links to track traffic sources accurately. These parameters enable precise attribution in Google Analytics and similar tools. Conversion tracking for specific actions like form submissions, sign-ups, or purchases. This tracking connects social media activities to business outcomes. Custom dashboards that visualize key metrics for different stakeholders. Executive dashboards might focus on high-level ROI, while tactical dashboards provide detailed content performance data. Thoughtful social media analytics transforms data into actionable insights that continuously improve your management approach. The Future of Social Media Management Social media management continues to evolve rapidly. Understanding emerging trends helps organizations prepare for future changes rather than merely reacting to them. Several key developments are reshaping how brands approach social media management: AI and Automation Integration Artificial intelligence is transforming social media management workflows. From content creation assistance to predictive analytics, AI tools are becoming essential for efficiency and effectiveness. Content generation AI helps teams produce more variations for testing while maintaining brand voice consistency. These tools are particularly valuable for creating first drafts that human creators then refine. AI-powered analytics reveal insights humans might miss by identifying patterns across vast datasets. These capabilities enable more sophisticated strategy refinement based on predictive rather than merely descriptive analytics. Conversation automation through chatbots and AI assistants helps teams manage increasing message volumes while maintaining response speed. The most effective implementations blend automation with human oversight. Social Commerce Expansion The line between social media and e-commerce continues to blur. This convergence transforms social platforms from awareness channels into complete shopping environments. In-app purchasing features eliminate friction between discovery and purchase. As these capabilities expand across platforms, social media managers increasingly need e-commerce expertise. With 246 million Americans (72.5% of the population) using social media, the potential audience for social commerce continues to grow. Product tagging, shoppable posts, and integrated checkout processes require new management approaches combining traditional social engagement with retail merchandising principles. Video Dominance and New Formats Video content continues gaining prominence across all major platforms. Short-form vertical video in particular has transformed content strategies for brands of all sizes. Live streaming offers authenticity and real-time engagement opportunities. Effective management now includes developing capabilities for quality live production and audience interaction. Interactive video formats like polls, quizzes, and shoppable elements create new engagement possibilities. These formats require both technical knowledge and creative thinking to implement effectively. Privacy Changes and First-Party Data Privacy regulations and platform changes are restricting data availability. This shift requires new approaches to audience targeting and measurement. First-party data strategies become essential as third-party tracking faces limitations. Social media managers now need to develop direct relationships that generate owned data. Community building takes priority over pure audience size. Private groups, messaging, and other controlled environments offer deeper engagement opportunities as public feeds face algorithmic challenges. To prepare for these evolving trends, social media managers should: Develop skills in emerging areas like AI prompt engineering and video production Build first-party data collection mechanisms like social-exclusive content offers Experiment with new formats early while they face less competition Focus on community quality metrics over simple reach measures The most successful organizations view these changes as opportunities rather than challenges. By anticipating shifts and adapting proactively, they gain competitive advantages while others scramble to catch up. Frequently Asked Questions What is the difference between social media management and social media marketing? Social media marketing is the strategy layer: goals, audience, platform choice, content pillars, and paid campaigns. Social media management is the execution layer: scheduling posts, replying to comments, and running the daily operation. In a small business, one person usually does both, but the distinction matters the moment you start hiring or budgeting. For the full breakdown, see my guide on what social media marketing is . Do small businesses really need a dedicated social media manager? Not always. In a small business, one capable generalist can cover strategy, content, and engagement, especially with the right tools handling scheduling and analytics. The tipping point comes when the workload across multiple platforms starts crowding out the strategic work, which is usually the signal to add specialized help or outsource. How much time does social media management actually take? More than most people expect. Beyond the visible posting, the hours go into planning, content creation, replying to comments and messages, monitoring mentions, and pulling reports. A single well-run platform can consume several hours a week once you include engagement and analysis, which is why so many teams lean on management tools to reclaim time. Can AI handle social media management on its own? Not on its own, at least not yet. AI now assists with drafting content, surfacing patterns in analytics, and automating routine replies, and a majority of marketers already use AI-powered tools in their workflows. The strongest setups still pair that automation with human judgment on strategy, brand voice, and anything sensitive like a crisis. What skills does a good social media manager need? A mix of creative and analytical ones. On the creative side: writing, visual content, and a feel for each platform’s culture. On the analytical side: reading metrics, connecting activity to business goals, and adjusting based on what the data shows. The best managers also stay curious, because platforms and formats change constantly. Conclusion Effective social media management extends far beyond simply posting content. It encompasses strategic planning, content creation, community engagement, analytics, and paid media optimization working together cohesively. As we’ve explored, the components of social media management form an interconnected system. Strategy informs content, which drives engagement, which generates data, which refines strategy in a continuous improvement cycle. For business leaders, understanding social media management’s true scope helps properly resource this function. The multidisciplinary nature of social media requires adequate investment in both tools and talent. For practitioners, approaching social media as a comprehensive management discipline rather than a set of tactical activities elevates the impact and perceived value of your work. This perspective connects social efforts to business outcomes. Whether you manage social media internally or partner with specialists, the principles remain the same. Clear objectives, audience understanding, strategic planning, and consistent execution drive meaningful results. As social platforms continue evolving, so too will management approaches. By building a solid foundation in these core principles while remaining adaptable to emerging trends, you position your organization for ongoing social media success. Get started now Social media is so much more than posting Twitter, Facebook, and LinkedIn updates. Before it was dubbed “social media,” it was known as “community management.” As an expert who led social media for small businesses in 2008, I’ll explain everything you should know about effective social media management. I’ve crafted this guide for small business owners and new marketing staffers who need to develop a social media strategy and get their organization firing on all eight cylinders regarding social media channels. What Is Social Media Management? Social media management is the process of planning, creating, and publishing content across social networks to grow a brand’s online presence . Managing social media involves educating stakeholders, developing a marketing strategy, and establishing governance to ensure a brand’s voice and customer experience are conveyed across social media channels. Included as essential parts of social media management are the following functions: Social media and marketing integration Business and platform-specific content plan Social media performance analysis Planning and creating content across multiple platforms Website content promotion Personalized customer support Brand and review monitoring Overseeing training and social workflows That sounds like a lot, doesn’t it? This is why social media responsibilities are often split among several members. In a small business or startup, this might be one person (or the business owner). You need social media management to guide the organization through social media and reach a targeted audience with engaging content and personalized support. Unlike 15 years ago, you shouldn’t automate your social media campaigns. It’s a bad look and ineffective at persuading your audience to care about your brand and take action. Social media is the catalyst for multiple marketing strategies (via Gartner) Real talk: Your business should be on social media because your customers want you there, and there’s a specific business objective behind it. If neither is true, you probably don’t need social media management. Related Article Best Social Media Monitoring Tools To Track Your Brand (And Competitors) Danny Grainger Elements of a Social Media Marketing Strategy An effective social media strategy aligns with the brand’s overall marketing objectives and business goals. Here are some key elements to consider for your social media marketing strategy: Target audiences and personas Analyze your existing customer demographics and create detailed buyer personas to determine your ideal customers on social media. Identify their age, location, gender, interests, pain points, and motivations. It’s imperative to understand your audience’s media consumption habits. Refrain from making big bets based on hypotheticals (I’ve been burned before). Talk to your customers on the phone , get to know them as people, how they research brands, and why they use social media. With this knowledge in hand, you’ll be ahead of 75% of others in the industry. Target like a media buyer Media buyers carefully consider how to reach their audience with a clear message. The goal is to stay top of mind with your targeted audience without necessarily expecting a quick ROI but engaging them with memorable ideas, strong visuals, and quick reminders of your brand. Paid social campaigns require more than just boosting existing posts. You want to be ruthless about audience selection and engagement. Otherwise, you’ll spend thousands of dollars on bots and unqualified visitors clicking your ads. Rather than rely solely on one platform, consider spreading your social media advertising across a few platforms for maximum reach. GaleForce Digital Technologies suggests thinking through your campaign’s demographics, creative assets, and performance metrics to be successful. Relevant social media platforms Research each social media platform and select the ones where your target audience is most active. Top platforms include Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, LinkedIn, YouTube, and TikTok. Consider emerging platforms as well. Instagram and Facebook are rated as the most effective for social media ROI (via HubSpot ) By default, you might feel you need to be everywhere. You don’t need to. If nothing else, claim your brand before someone squats on your name. Follow the money and the market. Where are your prospects? Where do customers spend most of their time? If it’s Twitter or Instagram, great. But if they primarily use LinkedIn, tailor your social media content plan around that platform. Lastly, try to enjoy how a social network functions as a user before going full throttle with marketing messages. There’s a little truth to marketers ruining everything . Social listening and customer support It’s crucial to set up listening tools to be responsive to inbound questions from customers and prospects. Connect every social media profile you have into one management tool. Prepare a plan for how you’ll handle complaints and compliments. A smart strategy is to go from public to direct messages to provide customer service. Over time, report on the number of brand mentions and specific campaigns stemming from your marketing efforts. Social media management tools can notify you of the growth or decline across your social media presence. Setting measurable goals Depending on your use case or stage of your business, you might not need metrics. Hear me out for a second. It’s okay to explore and experiment on social media. There is no surefire template or benchmark you need to hit to prove value in your business. Figure out what makes some brands more attractive than a pack of Double Stuffed Oreos. What are the underlying dynamics — is it the graphics, the advice, or are prominent influencers juicing up the algorithm? Without a big audience, you will need to be creative. You will likely need to invest in promoting your social media channels. You will also need to leverage platforms such as email, video, and even your phone system. With that said, you’ll want to consider the industry and competitors when setting targets for your social media marketing program. With defined business goals and KPIs in mind, you can analyze the effectiveness of your social media efforts. For instance, followers matter when your audience matches your ideal customer profile, but don’t do anything unnatural to play the system. Consider tracking engagement, traffic, and even share of voice (market share) on a given social network. Content strategy and posting schedule At this point, you should know a few key items: your ideal customers, what they consume on social media, and your overarching business goals. These help you craft a well-rounded content strategy for your business on social media. Now is the time to hit the brakes and think about the purpose behind your social media content. It should not be to generate leads or sales. Yes, you read that right. The goal behind your content is to be memorable and helpful to your audience. You don’t do that with gated webinars and whitepapers. Instead, focus on understanding the core reasons why people are interested in your product or service. Trusted marketing advisor Gaetano DiNardi draws a line in the sand regarding “demand capture” and “demand creation.” You need both, but social media should be utilized to build genuine interest, trust, and affinity for your brand. Digital marketing has transitioned from direct response, lead generation-focused marketing campaigns to a demand generation approach that covers brand awareness, demand creation, and demand capturing across the entire sales funnel. Gaetano DiNardi , Demand Generation Expert Having that said, here are the types of social media content to post: Hot takes on what’s happening in the industry Tips and tutorials to solve specific pain points Videos showing your solution or product at work Casual interviews with top industry voices Carousels and slides with original research and points of view Customer stories and case studies with real faces and logos Sneak peeks of your most recent email newsletter Takeaways from conferences and industry events Polls and genuine questions to ask your target audience Unexpected moments of brilliance and creativity Memes, newsjacking, and divisive topics, but proceed with caution The content to post shouldn’t deviate much from your current content strategy. Keep in mind that the goal is to earn trust and be memorable. When prospects realize they have a need, they’ll come back to you. With a rough list of content ideas, map them out for each platform. Give yourself the flexibility not to post daily, but stick to a consistent cadence. Each blog post you publish can be atomized or broken down into smaller assets so you can share various components that fit each social platform. You ought to ensure each post is optimized for your target audience so they can consume it easily without a high commitment. Video-first social media content Video is so important; you must be proactive with ideation, production, and distribution. Social media platforms are increasingly rewarding video content. Whether you build up your audience, educate your customers, or post Stories and Shorts, video is no longer optional. Invest in building out your video team agencies alike. Align your video creation with your brand identity with a high-quality video. Focus on being valuable, authentic, and visually appealing. While videos don’t have to be the center of your social media plan , they should still be a key component. Utilizing paid social ads Another area to consider is paid or performance marketing campaigns across social media. Most companies that want to grow will need additional social media advertising to distribute content to their audience. Share of marketing budget based on program spend (via Gartner) Take all your insights about your current customers and channel them into your paid social strategy. You don’t want to burn your budget on reaching “anyone in the U.S. 18+” as you’ll get nowhere. To be cost-effective, narrow your audience and set a daily budget. Consider starting with a remarketed audience until you nail down your brand’s social media campaigns. Type of content to use for paid social: Insightful case studies and customer testimonials Video-based product tours with helpful context Deep dives into how to do something faster or easier with your brand Atomized blog content with a call to action to continue reading Recycle previously successful organic (unpaid) social media content Social Media Management Best Practices Setting up profiles is just the start. Managing your accounts and interacting with your followers is crucial for social media success. Monitor notifications: Monitor all mentions, comments, shares, and direct messages to identify opportunities for engagement. Post consistently: Follow your content calendar to post regularly across your social media networks without long gaps between updates. Implement a workflow: Develop processes between team members to streamline community management. Use content creation tools: Social media management tools like Nextiva or Hootsuite help teams schedule posts, engage with followers, and monitor brand mentions. Analyze past content: Identify post content that resonated well on social media platforms and recycle it in your scheduling tool. By following thoughtful content marketing practices, your small team can actively manage growing social media communities as you expand your reach. Remember that social media interactions are public, and potential customers are watching. Be cordial, prompt, and direct. The last thing you want is to copy and paste responses to people. Types of Social Media Analytics There are a plethora of built-in and third-party analytics tools to help track the performance of your social media efforts. Monitoring key metrics and optimizing based on insights is crucial. Audience growth — Are your follower numbers consistently increasing? Does the audience resemble your ideal customer? Engagement rate — Is your audience reacting to the content you post? This metric is expressed as a percentage of your reach. Impressions — Was your content seen in your audience’s news feeds? Reach — How many unique people could your social media content reach? Website clicks — How much traffic is being driven to your site from social media? This metric isn’t always a good measure of success — think about your campaign objectives. Conversions — When creating demand, you’ll begin attracting higher-intent leads. How many resulted in leads, pipelines, or sales from social media? Look at performance trends over time and optimize your strategy accordingly. Consider analytics capabilities within your social media management software like Nextiva. Set up automated reports and dedicate time each month or look back at past data to achieve social media ROI. Social Media Management Tools Managing multiple social media accounts, engaging consistently with your community, and tracking performance is difficult without utilizing specialized social media management tools. The primary benefit of a social media management tool is that it’s engineered to work with each social network for analytics, publishing, and even removals. It helps your team work from one dashboard instead of several distinct workflows. We recommend budgeting approximately $300 per month for the best social media management tools and services. Plan for roughly $129 per month per user as your team grows. Here are a few top picks: Nextiva —In addition to its highly rated cloud PBX platform, Nextiva offers a social media management solution for customer service and marketing teams. It includes many advanced features for a flat monthly price. AgoraPulse — Ideal for businesses, especially those working with a lot of paid media and having to do content moderation. Like Nextiva, it also offers a unified social inbox, social listening, and reporting tools. Sprout Social — Good for larger organizations and agencies with a rigorous approval workflow. Includes employee advocacy and brand monitoring capabilities. The right social media management tool will optimize workflows, engagement, and analysis for an effective social media strategy . Consider both your budget and social media scheduling needs. Final Thoughts on Social Media Management A strategic approach to social media management is key for small businesses looking to drive brand awareness, website traffic, leads, and sales. Social media has evolved a lot over the last 15 years. Your social media strategy endures and has room to adapt to changes in the market. Pay attention to platform changes, user feedback, and your business’s practical needs. Set relevant and attainable goals, invest in high-quality content, and set up the proper internal workflows so you can support customers and weather the storm when crises emerge. Managing social media effectively is one of the top ways to bring your marketing strategy to life and scale your brand. Today, your business can engage directly with customers to uncover valuable insights about them, handle complaints, and develop a stronger value proposition by putting the customer at the heart of everything you do. However, managing social media can be a daunting task without the right strategy and tools. Social media management touches on a number of important elements, all of which form part of a well-structured digital marketing strategy. Best Practices for Social Media Management Conclusion What Is Social Media Management? Simply put, it's the process of managing a complete social media strategy. But social media management is a little more strategic. It involves more than just replying to tweets and comments. Erik Qualman , the author of Socialnomics, says, " We don't have a choice on whether we do social media; the question is, how well we do it. " That's exactly what social media encompasses; the doing part of social media. It starts with creating a social media strategy, implementing it, and then managing the day-to-day activities on various social media platforms. Beth Comstock , Vice-Chair of GE, puts it quite well, "Marketing's job is never done. It's about perpetual motion. We must continue to innovate every day . " With this in mind, if we look at social media management on a more minute scale, it involves a continuous process of creating, publishing, analyzing, and engaging with content on social media platforms. It could be something as simple as replying to a follower's comment or as complex as creating a full-blown social media campaign. Besides social media channels, this process also entails other verticals, such as: Online reputation management Paid social media advertising Social media analytics Community management Social listening and monitoring Evolution of Social Media Management Many years ago, when social media originated, its management wasn't as complex as it is today. Back in the day, brands could create a social media page and add content occasionally, and that would suffice. However, as social media usage increased, so did the number of channels and their conventions. Take Victoria's Secret as an example. The brand has been on social media for years. Initially, Victoria's Secret only had a Facebook and an Instagram page. Both channels worked well for them, with the former having 29 million followers and the latter 76 million. The brand mainly posted about its promotions, new products, sales, or celebrity endorsements. Victoria's Secret’s content was aesthetically pleasing, with models donning lingerie and a few videos of the annual fashion show. Fast forward to today, Victoria's Secret has a presence on more platforms, such as TikTok . The kind of content the company posts has also evolved over time. @victoriassecret Now, it's common to see influencer campaigns and user-generated content on the brand's social media pages. Victoria's Secret has also added a link to its shop on Instagram and other platforms to capitalize on social commerce. @victoriassecret See you in the front row, @Brittany Xavier. #VSFestivalSeason #FestivalOutfit ♬ Saturn X Slow Dancing In The Dark - reavesaudios Besides the content type and availability of platforms, social media has also changed in terms of analytics . Now, marketers have more data to work with. AI predictive analysis tools and social listening software are also available to find the tiniest insights previously overlooked. Similarly, personalization has found its place in social media marketing. Instead of creating the same content for everyone, brands now cater to separate audience segments to keep everyone engaged. There was a time when Victoria's Secret was only thought to be for a certain body type. However, now, the company celebrates body positivity and diversity, thanks to the insights gathered from social media. For example, a Mother's Day campaign run by Victoria's Secret on TikTok and Instagram showed the company's inclusivity for "mom bods." @victoriassecret From a growing belly to their newborn bubble all new moms want (and deserve) to be comfy. #VSMothersDay #MothersDay #Gift ♬ This Will Be - audios4you As social media evolves, so should brands. That's the only way to remain abreast of the competition and cater to changing consumer demands. Roles and Responsibilities of a Social Media Manager According to Indeed data, social media managers in the US make $57,463 per month . While this is the average, the salary can go up to $93,553 on the higher end and $35,295 on the lower end. Social media manager salary in the US So, what does a social media manager do to earn this amount of money? Let's look at some of the key roles and responsibilities. Social media strategy creation and execution: It includes creating a strategy, selecting the channels to use, and executing the plan. Some tasks may involve creating a content calendar, managing budgets for paid ads, etc. Social media platform management: It involves creating content, publishing posts, running campaigns, responding to comments, and partnering with influencers. Social media analytics: The manager analyzes social media metrics and provides insights on how to improve engagement and drive more traffic. Competitive analysis: Knowing what the competitors are doing is instrumental to a brand's success on social media. Audience engagement: It includes responding to comments and messages or hosting giveaways. Indeed, data further shows that the top skill for social media management is social listening. An understanding of media buying can increase salary prospects by 40.09%, indicating the importance of social commerce. Skills for social media management It’s important for your social media manager to have most, if not all, of these skills. Otherwise, as Stuart Davidson says, ‘’ If you think it’s expensive to hire a social media professional, just wait until you hire an amateur. ’’ Importance of Effective Social Media Management for Aspiring Social Media Managers Social media management is important for every business, irrespective of size and industry.
